name: South African Sign Language
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
sweep_summary: South African Sign Language is not in the catalog and, being a signed language, has no word-stress-placement literature. All 20 stress/prosody-titled items that Glottolog 5.1 attaches to sout1404 are keyword noise triggered by 'visual' (spoken-language audiovisual prosody, infant word learning, eye tracking, NLP, reading discomfort, a Praat script) or concern other sign languages (Dachkovsky & Sandler 2009 on Israeli SL intonation, abstract read via Europe PMC; Sandler, Belsitzman & Meir 2020 on ABSL/ISL foreign accent, abstract read; Sandler 2012 'Visual prosody' handbook chapter, closed access, not read). None says anything about SASL. The only SASL-specific phonology paper found (Sibanda & Siyavoshi 2025, toponyms, 'framed within the prosodic model') is abstract-only: the T&F PDF is behind a bot-check although Unpaywall marks it OA; its abstract contains no stress statement. Of the four SASL theses already held by the project from the earlier reading, only Prinsloo 2003 mentions stress: compound reduction ('the first sign loses stress', a BSL-derived generalisation, p. 49) and emphatic stress in commands with SASL examples *SIT*, *EAT*, *GO* (p. 72) - not lexical stress placement. Nothing to acquire with priority above low; no best new statement. Records saved and logged in

sources.quote: Signed languages use stress (emphasis) and usually direct eye-gaze towards the addressee to indicate a command (Baker-Schenk & Cokely, 1994:139). [...] The symbol * is used to indicate an imperative. When a sign is stressed, an asterisk is written after the sign (Valli & Lucas, 1995:141). Examples of stressed commands in SASL are *SIT* (Fig.5.7), *EAT* and *GO*.
sources.locator: p. 72 (PDF p. 79), section 5 on imperatives; compounding passage p. 49 (PDF p. 56)
sources.note: Ch. 3 Phonology (pp. 18-27) covers the five sign parameters (handshape, palm orientation, movement, location, non-manual signals), minimal pairs, assimilation and the Stokoe / Liddell-Johnson models; nothing on word stress. 'Stress' appears only in the compounding section (p. 49): 'Reduction also occurs as the first sign loses stress and both the first and second signs lose repetition (Sutton-Spence & Woll, 1999:102)'; in the morphology conclusion (p. 50): spoken languages 'change the stress of the word', signed languages use internal inflection/reduplication instead; and for imperatives (p.…
